- Nigel Mansell (9 points) - British
- Alain Prost (6 points) - French
- Nelson Piquet (4 points) - Brazilian
- Keke Rosberg (3 points) - Finnish
- René Arnoux (2 points) - French

### 1988 French Grand Prix (Points awarded: 9, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1 for positions 1-6)

- Alain Prost (9 points) - French
- Ayrton Senna (6 points) - Brazilian
- Michele Alboreto (4 points) - Italian
- Gerhard Berger (3 points) - Austrian

| Driver | Nationality | 1986 Points | 1988 Points |
|--------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| **Alain Prost** | 🇫🇷 French | 6 | 9 |
| **Nelson Piquet** | 🇧🇷 Brazilian | 4 | 2 |

Only these two drivers scored more than one point in both races, making them the only ones whose nationalities meet your criteria.

# Alain Prost
## Honda F1
### Legendary F1 Drivers
Known as “The Professor,” Alain Prost was one of Formula 1®’s defining figures of the 1980s and early 1990s.
Renowned for his intelligent, methodical approach to racing,
he claimed four World Championships and established himself as one of the sport’s greatest drivers.
His rivalry with Ayrton Senna at McLaren Honda in 1988 remains one of the most celebrated chapters in F1 history.
As McLaren Honda dominated the season with 15 victories from 16 races,
Prost’s only true rival was his teammate.
Their battle intensified throughout the year, evolving into a fierce championship fight.
Prost ultimately scored more points through remarkable consistency, recording seven victories and seven second-place finishes.
However, under the championship’s drop-score system, the title went to Senna.
The outcome became a defining moment in the deterioration of their relationship.
Despite their contrasting personalities and driving styles, Prost and Senna pushed each other to extraordinary heights.
Their rivalry continued even after Prost left McLaren, and from 1988 to 1990 the two drivers defined F1.
The period is still remembered as the “Senna and Prost era.”

# Alain Prost
## **C**areer
Born in France in 1955, Alain Prost originally dreamed of becoming a professional football player. His life changed at the age of 14 when he discovered karting, a chance encounter that set him on a path toward motorsport.
Prost quickly established himself as one of Europe’s leading kart racers. After winning the European Junior Kart Championship in 1972, he claimed further titles in higher karting categories before moving into single-seater racing.
In 1976, he entered the French Formula Renault Championship and dominated the series, winning 12 of 13 races to secure the title. He stepped up to the European Formula Renault Championship in 1977 and again emerged champion, claiming six victories.
Prost moved into the European Formula 3 Championship in 1978. Although his first season produced modest results, he returned in 1979 to win nine of 13 races and secure the championship, opening the door to F1.
Initially hoping to join the French Ligier team, Prost instead signed with McLaren and made his F1 debut in 1980. Despite scoring points in his first race, McLaren was going through a difficult period, prompting Prost to move to the Renault factory team.
Driving for Renault in 1981, Prost secured his first F1 victory at the French Grand Prix. He won three races that season and stood on the podium six times, although reliability problems resulted in numerous retirements. During his three years with Renault, Prost established himself as a title contender but fell just short of championship success.
During this period he also experienced personal and professional challenges. His close friends Gilles Villeneuve and Didier Pironi became embroiled in a bitter rivalry at Ferrari that ended in tragedy, with Villeneuve losing his life and Pironi suffering career-ending injuries. The events are widely regarded as having had a profound influence on Prost’s outlook on both life and racing.
Returning to McLaren in 1984, Prost partnered two-time World Champion Niki Lauda. The championship quickly became a duel between the pair. Prost often displayed superior speed, while Lauda accumulated points through relentless consistency. Ultimately, Lauda claimed the title by the narrowest margin in F1 history, and Prost finished runner-up. The experience shaped Prost’s approach, encouraging him to become an even more calculated and strategic driver.

# Alain Prost
## Honda F1
### Legendary F1 Drivers
Known as “The Professor,” Alain Prost was one of Formula 1®’s defining figures of the 1980s and early 1990s.
Renowned for his intelligent, methodical approach to racing,
he claimed four World Championships and established himself as one of the sport’s greatest drivers.
His rivalry with Ayrton Senna at McLaren Honda in 1988 remains one of the most celebrated chapters in F1 history.
As McLaren Honda dominated the season with 15 victories from 16 races,
Prost’s only true rival was his teammate.
Their battle intensified throughout the year, evolving into a fierce championship fight.
Prost ultimately scored more points through remarkable consistency, recording seven victories and seven second-place finishes.
However, under the championship’s drop-score system, the title went to Senna.
The outcome became a defining moment in the deterioration of their relationship.
Despite their contrasting personalities and driving styles, Prost and Senna pushed each other to extraordinary heights.
Their rivalry continued even after Prost left McLaren, and from 1988 to 1990 the two drivers defined F1.
The period is still remembered as the “Senna and Prost era.”

# Alain Prost
## **C**areer
Born in France in 1955, Alain Prost originally dreamed of becoming a professional football player. His life changed at the age of 14 when he discovered karting, a chance encounter that set him on a path toward motorsport.
Prost quickly established himself as one of Europe’s leading kart racers. After winning the European Junior Kart Championship in 1972, he claimed further titles in higher karting categories before moving into single-seater racing.
In 1976, he entered the French Formula Renault Championship and dominated the series, winning 12 of 13 races to secure the title. He stepped up to the European Formula Renault Championship in 1977 and again emerged champion, claiming six victories.
Prost moved into the European Formula 3 Championship in 1978. Although his first season produced modest results, he returned in 1979 to win nine of 13 races and secure the championship, opening the door to F1.
Initially hoping to join the French Ligier team, Prost instead signed with McLaren and made his F1 debut in 1980. Despite scoring points in his first race, McLaren was going through a difficult period, prompting Prost to move to the Renault factory team.
Driving for Renault in 1981, Prost secured his first F1 victory at the French Grand Prix. He won three races that season and stood on the podium six times, although reliability problems resulted in numerous retirements. During his three years with Renault, Prost established himself as a title contender but fell just short of championship success.
During this period he also experienced personal and professional challenges. His close friends Gilles Villeneuve and Didier Pironi became embroiled in a bitter rivalry at Ferrari that ended in tragedy, with Villeneuve losing his life and Pironi suffering career-ending injuries. The events are widely regarded as having had a profound influence on Prost’s outlook on both life and racing.
Returning to McLaren in 1984, Prost partnered two-time World Champion Niki Lauda. The championship quickly became a duel between the pair. Prost often displayed superior speed, while Lauda accumulated points through relentless consistency. Ultimately, Lauda claimed the title by the narrowest margin in F1 history, and Prost finished runner-up. The experience shaped Prost’s approach, encouraging him to become an even more calculated and strategic driver.

### Legendary F1 Drivers
Known as “The Professor,” Alain Prost was one of Formula 1®’s defining figures of the 1980s and early 1990s.
Renowned for his intelligent, methodical approach to racing,
he claimed four World Championships and established himself as one of the sport’s greatest drivers.
His rivalry with Ayrton Senna at McLaren Honda in 1988 remains one of the most celebrated chapters in F1 history.
As McLaren Honda dominated the season with 15 victories from 16 races,
Prost’s only true rival was his teammate.
Their battle intensified throughout the year, evolving into a fierce championship fight.
Prost ultimately scored more points through remarkable consistency, recording seven victories and seven second-place finishes.
However, under the championship’s drop-score system, the title went to Senna.
The outcome became a defining moment in the deterioration of their relationship.
Despite their contrasting personalities and driving styles, Prost and Senna pushed each other to extraordinary heights.
Their rivalry continued even after Prost left McLaren, and from 1988 to 1990 the two drivers defined F1.
The period is still remembered as the “Senna and Prost era.”

# Alain Prost
## **C**areer
Born in France in 1955, Alain Prost originally dreamed of becoming a professional football player. His life changed at the age of 14 when he discovered karting, a chance encounter that set him on a path toward motorsport.
Prost quickly established himself as one of Europe’s leading kart racers. After winning the European Junior Kart Championship in 1972, he claimed further titles in higher karting categories before moving into single-seater racing.
In 1976, he entered the French Formula Renault Championship and dominated the series, winning 12 of 13 races to secure the title. He stepped up to the European Formula Renault Championship in 1977 and again emerged champion, claiming six victories.
Prost moved into the European Formula 3 Championship in 1978. Although his first season produced modest results, he returned in 1979 to win nine of 13 races and secure the championship, opening the door to F1.
Initially hoping to join the French Ligier team, Prost instead signed with McLaren and made his F1 debut in 1980. Despite scoring points in his first race, McLaren was going through a difficult period, prompting Prost to move to the Renault factory team.
Driving for Renault in 1981, Prost secured his first F1 victory at the French Grand Prix. He won three races that season and stood on the podium six times, although reliability problems resulted in numerous retirements. During his three years with Renault, Prost established himself as a title contender but fell just short of championship success.
During this period he also experienced personal and professional challenges. His close friends Gilles Villeneuve and Didier Pironi became embroiled in a bitter rivalry at Ferrari that ended in tragedy, with Villeneuve losing his life and Pironi suffering career-ending injuries. The events are widely regarded as having had a profound influence on Prost’s outlook on both life and racing.
Returning to McLaren in 1984, Prost partnered two-time World Champion Niki Lauda. The championship quickly became a duel between the pair. Prost often displayed superior speed, while Lauda accumulated points through relentless consistency. Ultimately, Lauda claimed the title by the narrowest margin in F1 history, and Prost finished runner-up. The experience shaped Prost’s approach, encouraging him to become an even more calculated and strategic driver.

HALL OF FAME - 1981, 1983, 1987
He was never a dominant driver but a crafty expert in winning by stealth, according to his detractors. He admitted he was lazy, yet willingly worked hard to improve his car. He could be cold and cruel but could also be warm and funny. He hated being a celebrity yet lived the life of a playboy to the hilt. He was never hugely popular but couldn't care less. All Nelson Piquet really cared about was driving a racing car, which he loved with a passion, especially when he won, which he did often enough to become a triple World Champion.
Born Nelson Sautomaior, on August 17, 1952, he used his mother's surname Piquet to hide his early racing adventures from his disapproving parents. His father, a prominent Brazilian government minister, had been a regional tennis champion and when Nelson showed early promise in that sport he was encouraged to pursue it. At 12 he was one of Brazil's most promising junior prospects. At 16, to further hone his tennis skills, his parents enrolled him at a school in California. But whacking a ball around a tennis court began to take second place in Nelson's mind to driving a car around a race track, particularly when his countryman Emerson Fittipaldi started making inroads abroad. And so Nelson Piquet began racing in his home state of Brazilia. Winning championships in karts and sportscars failed to win over his parents, who sought to distract him by sending him to university. But studying philosophy, engineering and management proved no substitute for the lure of racing and Nelson dropped out after a year. He sold his road car to buy a Formula Vee and in 1977 became the Brazilian champion in that category.

On the advice of Emerson Fittipaldi his next career move was to Europe, where he arrived in 1977 with enough cash (L10,000) to embark on a Formula Three program. In 1978 victories in 13 of 26 races made him champion of one British F3 series and runner-up in another. Formula 1 teams were impressed and he was given outings in an Ensign and a privately entered McLaren before being hired by Brabham boss Bernie Ecclestone to serve as understudy to Niki Lauda for 1979. When the Austrian veteran walked away from Formula 1 racing at the end of that season the Brazilian newcomer became Brabham team leader by default. He was still learning on the job, but proved entirely up to the task of helping develop designer Gordan Murray's promising car and extracting the best performance from it. In 1980 Nelson won three races and finished second to Alan Jones in the championship. In 1981 his upward mobility continued and, with three more wins and a succession of high finishes in a brilliant Brabham BT49, he became World Champion.
His 1982 season, hampered by an unreliable new BMW turbo engine, produced only one win, though Piquet considered that Canadian Grand Prix victory the best of his career. Throughout the race an oil radiator subjected his feet to 100 degree temperatures that made him scream with pain. And yet the thrill of victory was always worth it for this driver who once confessed: "Winning is a feeling which you cannot imagine. I sometimes piss my pants on the slowing down lap." His sometimes outrageous comments would eventually get him into trouble, though never with the Brabham personnel, who in appreciation of his earthy humour and hard work set up The Nelson Piquet Fan Club.

In 1983 Piquet powered his turbo-charged BMW-Brabham BT52 to three race wins and, after a season-long battle with Renault's Alain Prost, sensationally snatched his second driving title. At this point, having grown tired of all the travel, Nelson considered retiring but was persuaded by the noted aviator Niki Lauda that a private jet would make it easier to enjoy private life. Thanks to his personal jet Nelson was able to enjoy more of his version of the good life. In the harbour at his Monaco base he kept an 18-meter motor yacht manned by a permanent crew and capable of cruising at 28 knots. On his much-loved Mediterranean voyages laid-back Nelson enjoyed swimming, water skiing, watching TV and entertaining a series of gorgeous female companions. With them he fathered several children and always provided for his extended family.
His costly lifestyle made making more money a priority and Nelson began looking for a better deal from Bernie Ecclestone. More championships might have helped the financial cause but the 1984 and 1985 Brabhams were far from world beaters. To continue with the team Nelson asked for his $1 million retainer to be doubled. While Ecclestone baulked at this Frank Williams offered to triple it and so began two tumultuous years at Williams-Honda. The car was a winner and so were the team's drivers: Nelson Piquet and Nigel Mansell. The problem was the team mates hated each other and in 1986 were so preoccupied with their personal feud that Alain Prost sneaked in and beat them both to the driving title. The bothered Brazilian accused Williams of favouring their British driver and tried to destabilize Mansell by publicly calling him "an uneducated blockhead" and defaming his wife. "Piquet is just a vile man," Mansell said.
In the 1987 edition of the Nigel versus Nelson conflict Mansell won more battles, (six wins to three) but Piquet won the war by means of a better finishing record that brought him his third driving title. Some critics decided his refusal to play a role in the showbiz aspect of his sport made him an unsatisfactory World Champion. "What do they mean by that?" Nelson wondered. "Do they mean doing a lot of publicity? I don't want to make friends with anybody. I don't give a shit for fame. I just want to win."

With few wins in his future his fame duly declined. He left Williams in a fit of pique and moved to Lotus for a couple of seasons at a time when the team was on the wane, then spent two years at Benetton where it was his motivation that waned. After winning twice in 1990 and once the next year he left Formula 1 racing at the age of 40, though he wasn't yet finished with motorsport.
An attempt to qualify for the 1992 Indianapolis 500 ended in the worst accident of his career, leaving him with badly crushed lower limbs. Thereafter he raced occasionally in Brazil and abroad in touring cars and long-distance events. He became a successful businessman in Brazil, establishing a satellite navigation company that earned him a fortune and enabled him to fully support the promising career of his son, Nelson Piquet Jr.

# Nelson Piquet
## **C**areer
Born in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 1952, Nelson Piquet began karting at the age of 14. He won the Brazilian Kart Championship in 1971 and successfully defended the title the following year.
In 1976, he captured the Brazilian Formula Vee championship before moving to Europe in 1977 to compete in the European Formula Three Championship. The move was reportedly supported by fellow Brazilian World Champion Emerson Fittipaldi. Although Piquet did not contest the full season, he won two races and finished third in the championship standings.
Piquet made his F1 debut at the 1978 German Grand Prix with Ensign. Although he retired from the race, his performance impressed Brabham team owner Bernie Ecclestone, who gave him an opportunity to drive for Brabham at the season-ending Canadian Grand Prix. That appearance secured him a full-time seat for 1979.
Despite being a rookie at Brabham, Piquet immediately demonstrated his speed. He qualified third at both the Belgian and British Grands Prix and quickly established himself as one of the sport’s most promising young talents. His first points came with a fourth-place finish at the Dutch Grand Prix.
In 1980, Piquet inherited the role of team leader following Niki Lauda’s surprise retirement during the previous season. Brabham switched to the highly competitive Cosworth DFV engine, and Piquet’s talent flourished. He became a championship contender, claiming his first F1 victory at the United States West Grand Prix in dominant fashion from pole position. Consistent results throughout the season kept him firmly in title contention. Although a costly retirement late in the year left him second in the championship, he scored points in 10 of the 14 races and reached the podium six times, including three victories.
Piquet entered 1981 determined to secure the championship that had narrowly escaped him. Combining race wins with consistent points finishes, he remained in contention throughout the season and ultimately overturned a one-point deficit at the final race in Las Vegas to become World Champion for the first time.

# Nelson Piquet
## **C**areer
Brabham adopted BMW turbo power in 1982 as F1 entered the turbo era, but the transition proved difficult. The team improved significantly in 1983, and despite appearing to lose ground to rivals during much of the season, Piquet mounted a late charge with consecutive victories to secure his second World Championship.
Piquet remained with Brabham for the following seasons, but the team’s competitiveness gradually declined relative to its rivals. Although he achieved a personal-best nine pole positions in 1984, he converted only two into victories. In 1985 he managed just two podium finishes and decided it was time for a change.
In 1986, Piquet joined Williams, which was powered by Honda’s increasingly dominant turbo engine. Honda strongly supported the signing of the experienced World Champion as it pursued its first championship titles. However, the season was overshadowed by a serious road accident involving team founder Frank Williams shortly before the opening race, creating significant changes within the organization. Tensions emerged between Mansell, Britain’s rising star and recent race winner, and Piquet, the established World Champion backed by Honda. The FW11 was exceptionally competitive, and Williams won nine of the season’s 16 races. Yet with Piquet claiming four victories and Mansell five, the two drivers effectively took points from one another, allowing the Drivers’ Championship to slip away despite securing the Constructors’ title.
The following year, Williams Honda became the benchmark of F1. Piquet demonstrated the consistency that had defined his career. While Mansell won six races, he also suffered several costly retirements. Piquet, by contrast, won only three races but scored points 12 times, including 11 podium finishes. His relentless consistency earned him a third World Championship. Honda secured both the Constructors’ and Drivers’ titles for the first time, proving the superiority of its engine package.

# Nelson Piquet
## **C**areer
During the 1987 Italian Grand Prix weekend, Honda announced that it would switch its engine supply from Williams to McLaren for 1988. As a result, Piquet moved to Lotus, which would continue to receive Honda engines. Although Honda power remained dominant, Lotus could not match the performance of McLaren. Piquet began the season with a series of podium finishes but was rarely in a position to challenge for victories. He finished sixth in the championship after scoring points seven times, a result that fell short of his expectations.
Piquet remained with Lotus in 1989 despite the team’s loss of Honda power. Competitiveness dropped dramatically, and after scoring points on only four occasions and failing to reach the podium, he finished eighth in the championship and chose to move to Benetton.
In 1990, Piquet signed an unusual performance-based contract with Benetton. He contributed significantly to the development of the team’s increasingly competitive cars and continued to produce strong results. His trademark consistency remained intact, and he finished third in the championship after winning two races and scoring points in 12 of the season’s 16 rounds.
Piquet stayed with Benetton in 1991 and added another victory at the Canadian Grand Prix. However, changes within the team prompted him to seek opportunities elsewhere. When negotiations with potential teams failed to produce a satisfactory agreement, he decided to retire from F1 at the end of the season.
Although he stepped away from F1™, Piquet announced plans to compete in the Indianapolis 500 in 1992. During practice before qualifying, he suffered a major accident that left him with multiple fractures in both legs. Undeterred, he underwent extensive rehabilitation and made a remarkable recovery, eventually returning to competition. He continued racing until 1998, including appearances in the South American Formula Three Championship, before retiring from driving altogether.
In 2000, Piquet’s achievements were formally recognized with his induction into the International Motorsports Hall of Fame.

• Happy birthday to Nelson Piquet: the irreverent genius who turned Formula 1 into a mechanical art form.
Three-time World Champion (1981, 1983, 1987), born in Rio de Janeiro on this very day in 1952. As a teenager he raced karts in secret, hiding his passion from his politician father, until Emerson Fittipaldi himself convinced him to chase his future in Europe.
Piquet wasn’t just fast, he read the car. Few drivers in history could adapt their style to a machine’s behaviour like he did, lap after lap, tenth after tenth.
His masterpiece of pure calculation came at Kyalami, 1983. Trailing Alain Prost going into the season finale, Piquet built a 30 second lead in the opening laps. Then, once he knew third place was enough, he deliberately backed off the turbo boost and waved his own teammates through, cruising to the title and becoming the first World Champion in history to win with a turbocharged engine, the legendary Brabham BMW BT52.

HALL OF FAME - 1981, 1983, 1987
He was never a dominant driver but a crafty expert in winning by stealth, according to his detractors. He admitted he was lazy, yet willingly worked hard to improve his car. He could be cold and cruel but could also be warm and funny. He hated being a celebrity yet lived the life of a playboy to the hilt. He was never hugely popular but couldn't care less. All Nelson Piquet really cared about was driving a racing car, which he loved with a passion, especially when he won, which he did often enough to become a triple World Champion.
Born Nelson Sautomaior, on August 17, 1952, he used his mother's surname Piquet to hide his early racing adventures from his disapproving parents. His father, a prominent Brazilian government minister, had been a regional tennis champion and when Nelson showed early promise in that sport he was encouraged to pursue it. At 12 he was one of Brazil's most promising junior prospects. At 16, to further hone his tennis skills, his parents enrolled him at a school in California. But whacking a ball around a tennis court began to take second place in Nelson's mind to driving a car around a race track, particularly when his countryman Emerson Fittipaldi started making inroads abroad. And so Nelson Piquet began racing in his home state of Brazilia. Winning championships in karts and sportscars failed to win over his parents, who sought to distract him by sending him to university. But studying philosophy, engineering and management proved no substitute for the lure of racing and Nelson dropped out after a year. He sold his road car to buy a Formula Vee and in 1977 became the Brazilian champion in that category.
texts.1:
On the advice of Emerson Fittipaldi his next career move was to Europe, where he arrived in 1977 with enough cash (L10,000) to embark on a Formula Three program. In 1978 victories in 13 of 26 races made him champion of one British F3 series and runner-up in another. Formula 1 teams were impressed and he was given outings in an Ensign and a privately entered McLaren before being hired by Brabham boss Bernie Ecclestone to serve as understudy to Niki Lauda for 1979. When the Austrian veteran walked away from Formula 1 racing at the end of that season the Brazilian newcomer became Brabham team leader by default. He was still learning on the job, but proved entirely up to the task of helping develop designer Gordan Murray's promising car and extracting the best performance from it. In 1980 Nelson won three races and finished second to Alan Jones in the championship. In 1981 his upward mobility continued and, with three more wins and a succession of high finishes in a brilliant Brabham BT49, he became World Champion.
His 1982 season, hampered by an unreliable new BMW turbo engine, produced only one win, though Piquet considered that Canadian Grand Prix victory the best of his career. Throughout the race an oil radiator subjected his feet to 100 degree temperatures that made him scream with pain. And yet the thrill of victory was always worth it for this driver who once confessed: "Winning is a feeling which you cannot imagine. I sometimes piss my pants on the slowing down lap." His sometimes outrageous comments would eventually get him into trouble, though never with the Brabham personnel, who in appreciation of his earthy humour and hard work set up The Nelson Piquet Fan Club.
texts.2:
In 1983 Piquet powered his turbo-charged BMW-Brabham BT52 to three race wins and, after a season-long battle with Renault's Alain Prost, sensationally snatched his second driving title. At this point, having grown tired of all the travel, Nelson considered retiring but was persuaded by the noted aviator Niki Lauda that a private jet would make it easier to enjoy private life. Thanks to his personal jet Nelson was able to enjoy more of his version of the good life. In the harbour at his Monaco base he kept an 18-meter motor yacht manned by a permanent crew and capable of cruising at 28 knots. On his much-loved Mediterranean voyages laid-back Nelson enjoyed swimming, water skiing, watching TV and entertaining a series of gorgeous female companions. With them he fathered several children and always provided for his extended family.
His costly lifestyle made making more money a priority and Nelson began looking for a better deal from Bernie Ecclestone. More championships might have helped the financial cause but the 1984 and 1985 Brabhams were far from world beaters. To continue with the team Nelson asked for his $1 million retainer to be doubled. While Ecclestone baulked at this Frank Williams offered to triple it and so began two tumultuous years at Williams-Honda. The car was a winner and so were the team's drivers: Nelson Piquet and Nigel Mansell. The problem was the team mates hated each other and in 1986 were so preoccupied with their personal feud that Alain Prost sneaked in and beat them both to the driving title. The bothered Brazilian accused Williams of favouring their British driver and tried to destabilize Mansell by publicly calling him "an uneducated blockhead" and defaming his wife. "Piquet is just a vile man," Mansell said.
In the 1987 edition of the Nigel versus Nelson conflict Mansell won more battles, (six wins to three) but Piquet won the war by means of a better finishing record that brought him his third driving title. Some critics decided his refusal to play a role in the showbiz aspect of his sport made him an unsatisfactory World Champion. "What do they mean by that?" Nelson wondered. "Do they mean doing a lot of publicity? I don't want to make friends with anybody. I don't give a shit for fame. I just want to win."
texts.3:
With few wins in his future his fame duly declined. He left Williams in a fit of pique and moved to Lotus for a couple of seasons at a time when the team was on the wane, then spent two years at Benetton where it was his motivation that waned. After winning twice in 1990 and once the next year he left Formula 1 racing at the age of 40, though he wasn't yet finished with motorsport.
An attempt to qualify for the 1992 Indianapolis 500 ended in the worst accident of his career, leaving him with badly crushed lower limbs. Thereafter he raced occasionally in Brazil and abroad in touring cars and long-distance events. He became a successful businessman in Brazil, establishing a satellite navigation company that earned him a fortune and enabled him to fully support the promising career of his son, Nelson Piquet Jr.
_Text - Gerald Donaldson_

# Nelson Piquet
## **C**areer
Born in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 1952, Nelson Piquet began karting at the age of 14. He won the Brazilian Kart Championship in 1971 and successfully defended the title the following year.
In 1976, he captured the Brazilian Formula Vee championship before moving to Europe in 1977 to compete in the European Formula Three Championship. The move was reportedly supported by fellow Brazilian World Champion Emerson Fittipaldi. Although Piquet did not contest the full season, he won two races and finished third in the championship standings.
Piquet made his F1 debut at the 1978 German Grand Prix with Ensign. Although he retired from the race, his performance impressed Brabham team owner Bernie Ecclestone, who gave him an opportunity to drive for Brabham at the season-ending Canadian Grand Prix. That appearance secured him a full-time seat for 1979.
Despite being a rookie at Brabham, Piquet immediately demonstrated his speed. He qualified third at both the Belgian and British Grands Prix and quickly established himself as one of the sport’s most promising young talents. His first points came with a fourth-place finish at the Dutch Grand Prix.
In 1980, Piquet inherited the role of team leader following Niki Lauda’s surprise retirement during the previous season. Brabham switched to the highly competitive Cosworth DFV engine, and Piquet’s talent flourished. He became a championship contender, claiming his first F1 victory at the United States West Grand Prix in dominant fashion from pole position. Consistent results throughout the season kept him firmly in title contention. Although a costly retirement late in the year left him second in the championship, he scored points in 10 of the 14 races and reached the podium six times, including three victories.
Piquet entered 1981 determined to secure the championship that had narrowly escaped him. Combining race wins with consistent points finishes, he remained in contention throughout the season and ultimately overturned a one-point deficit at the final race in Las Vegas to become World Champion for the first time.

# Nelson Piquet
## **C**areer
Brabham adopted BMW turbo power in 1982 as F1 entered the turbo era, but the transition proved difficult. The team improved significantly in 1983, and despite appearing to lose ground to rivals during much of the season, Piquet mounted a late charge with consecutive victories to secure his second World Championship.
Piquet remained with Brabham for the following seasons, but the team’s competitiveness gradually declined relative to its rivals. Although he achieved a personal-best nine pole positions in 1984, he converted only two into victories. In 1985 he managed just two podium finishes and decided it was time for a change.
In 1986, Piquet joined Williams, which was powered by Honda’s increasingly dominant turbo engine. Honda strongly supported the signing of the experienced World Champion as it pursued its first championship titles. However, the season was overshadowed by a serious road accident involving team founder Frank Williams shortly before the opening race, creating significant changes within the organization. Tensions emerged between Mansell, Britain’s rising star and recent race winner, and Piquet, the established World Champion backed by Honda. The FW11 was exceptionally competitive, and Williams won nine of the season’s 16 races. Yet with Piquet claiming four victories and Mansell five, the two drivers effectively took points from one another, allowing the Drivers’ Championship to slip away despite securing the Constructors’ title.
The following year, Williams Honda became the benchmark of F1. Piquet demonstrated the consistency that had defined his career. While Mansell won six races, he also suffered several costly retirements. Piquet, by contrast, won only three races but scored points 12 times, including 11 podium finishes. His relentless consistency earned him a third World Championship. Honda secured both the Constructors’ and Drivers’ titles for the first time, proving the superiority of its engine package.

# Nelson Piquet
## **C**areer
During the 1987 Italian Grand Prix weekend, Honda announced that it would switch its engine supply from Williams to McLaren for 1988. As a result, Piquet moved to Lotus, which would continue to receive Honda engines. Although Honda power remained dominant, Lotus could not match the performance of McLaren. Piquet began the season with a series of podium finishes but was rarely in a position to challenge for victories. He finished sixth in the championship after scoring points seven times, a result that fell short of his expectations.
Piquet remained with Lotus in 1989 despite the team’s loss of Honda power. Competitiveness dropped dramatically, and after scoring points on only four occasions and failing to reach the podium, he finished eighth in the championship and chose to move to Benetton.
In 1990, Piquet signed an unusual performance-based contract with Benetton. He contributed significantly to the development of the team’s increasingly competitive cars and continued to produce strong results. His trademark consistency remained intact, and he finished third in the championship after winning two races and scoring points in 12 of the season’s 16 rounds.
Piquet stayed with Benetton in 1991 and added another victory at the Canadian Grand Prix. However, changes within the team prompted him to seek opportunities elsewhere. When negotiations with potential teams failed to produce a satisfactory agreement, he decided to retire from F1 at the end of the season.
Although he stepped away from F1™, Piquet announced plans to compete in the Indianapolis 500 in 1992. During practice before qualifying, he suffered a major accident that left him with multiple fractures in both legs. Undeterred, he underwent extensive rehabilitation and made a remarkable recovery, eventually returning to competition. He continued racing until 1998, including appearances in the South American Formula Three Championship, before retiring from driving altogether.
In 2000, Piquet’s achievements were formally recognized with his induction into the International Motorsports Hall of Fame.

HALL OF FAME - 1981, 1983, 1987
He was never a dominant driver but a crafty expert in winning by stealth, according to his detractors. He admitted he was lazy, yet willingly worked hard to improve his car. He could be cold and cruel but could also be warm and funny. He hated being a celebrity yet lived the life of a playboy to the hilt. He was never hugely popular but couldn't care less. All Nelson Piquet really cared about was driving a racing car, which he loved with a passion, especially when he won, which he did often enough to become a triple World Champion.
Born Nelson Sautomaior, on August 17, 1952, he used his mother's surname Piquet to hide his early racing adventures from his disapproving parents. His father, a prominent Brazilian government minister, had been a regional tennis champion and when Nelson showed early promise in that sport he was encouraged to pursue it. At 12 he was one of Brazil's most promising junior prospects. At 16, to further hone his tennis skills, his parents enrolled him at a school in California. But whacking a ball around a tennis court began to take second place in Nelson's mind to driving a car around a race track, particularly when his countryman Emerson Fittipaldi started making inroads abroad. And so Nelson Piquet began racing in his home state of Brazilia. Winning championships in karts and sportscars failed to win over his parents, who sought to distract him by sending him to university. But studying philosophy, engineering and management proved no substitute for the lure of racing and Nelson dropped out after a year. He sold his road car to buy a Formula Vee and in 1977 became the Brazilian champion in that category.

On the advice of Emerson Fittipaldi his next career move was to Europe, where he arrived in 1977 with enough cash (L10,000) to embark on a Formula Three program. In 1978 victories in 13 of 26 races made him champion of one British F3 series and runner-up in another. Formula 1 teams were impressed and he was given outings in an Ensign and a privately entered McLaren before being hired by Brabham boss Bernie Ecclestone to serve as understudy to Niki Lauda for 1979. When the Austrian veteran walked away from Formula 1 racing at the end of that season the Brazilian newcomer became Brabham team leader by default. He was still learning on the job, but proved entirely up to the task of helping develop designer Gordan Murray's promising car and extracting the best performance from it. In 1980 Nelson won three races and finished second to Alan Jones in the championship. In 1981 his upward mobility continued and, with three more wins and a succession of high finishes in a brilliant Brabham BT49, he became World Champion.
His 1982 season, hampered by an unreliable new BMW turbo engine, produced only one win, though Piquet considered that Canadian Grand Prix victory the best of his career. Throughout the race an oil radiator subjected his feet to 100 degree temperatures that made him scream with pain. And yet the thrill of victory was always worth it for this driver who once confessed: "Winning is a feeling which you cannot imagine. I sometimes piss my pants on the slowing down lap." His sometimes outrageous comments would eventually get him into trouble, though never with the Brabham personnel, who in appreciation of his earthy humour and hard work set up The Nelson Piquet Fan Club.

In 1983 Piquet powered his turbo-charged BMW-Brabham BT52 to three race wins and, after a season-long battle with Renault's Alain Prost, sensationally snatched his second driving title. At this point, having grown tired of all the travel, Nelson considered retiring but was persuaded by the noted aviator Niki Lauda that a private jet would make it easier to enjoy private life. Thanks to his personal jet Nelson was able to enjoy more of his version of the good life. In the harbour at his Monaco base he kept an 18-meter motor yacht manned by a permanent crew and capable of cruising at 28 knots. On his much-loved Mediterranean voyages laid-back Nelson enjoyed swimming, water skiing, watching TV and entertaining a series of gorgeous female companions. With them he fathered several children and always provided for his extended family.
His costly lifestyle made making more money a priority and Nelson began looking for a better deal from Bernie Ecclestone. More championships might have helped the financial cause but the 1984 and 1985 Brabhams were far from world beaters. To continue with the team Nelson asked for his $1 million retainer to be doubled. While Ecclestone baulked at this Frank Williams offered to triple it and so began two tumultuous years at Williams-Honda. The car was a winner and so were the team's drivers: Nelson Piquet and Nigel Mansell. The problem was the team mates hated each other and in 1986 were so preoccupied with their personal feud that Alain Prost sneaked in and beat them both to the driving title. The bothered Brazilian accused Williams of favouring their British driver and tried to destabilize Mansell by publicly calling him "an uneducated blockhead" and defaming his wife. "Piquet is just a vile man," Mansell said.
In the 1987 edition of the Nigel versus Nelson conflict Mansell won more battles, (six wins to three) but Piquet won the war by means of a better finishing record that brought him his third driving title. Some critics decided his refusal to play a role in the showbiz aspect of his sport made him an unsatisfactory World Champion. "What do they mean by that?" Nelson wondered. "Do they mean doing a lot of publicity? I don't want to make friends with anybody. I don't give a shit for fame. I just want to win."

With few wins in his future his fame duly declined. He left Williams in a fit of pique and moved to Lotus for a couple of seasons at a time when the team was on the wane, then spent two years at Benetton where it was his motivation that waned. After winning twice in 1990 and once the next year he left Formula 1 racing at the age of 40, though he wasn't yet finished with motorsport.
An attempt to qualify for the 1992 Indianapolis 500 ended in the worst accident of his career, leaving him with badly crushed lower limbs. Thereafter he raced occasionally in Brazil and abroad in touring cars and long-distance events. He became a successful businessman in Brazil, establishing a satellite navigation company that earned him a fortune and enabled him to fully support the promising career of his son, Nelson Piquet Jr.
